parameters.name: table
parameters.description: The table to iterate over. Every row is visited once and the expression is evaluated in that row's context.
parameters.examNote: Use FILTER() to limit the rows before averaging. AVERAGEX(FILTER(Sales, Sales[Region] = 'East'), ...) averages only East region rows.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: The expression evaluated for each row. The results from all rows are averaged. Blank results are excluded from the average calculation.
parameters.examNote: If the expression returns BLANK for some rows, those rows are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator of the average. This differs from treating blanks as zero.

returnType: Decimal (average of all non-blank per-row expression results)
summary: AVERAGEX iterates every row of a table, evaluates an expression for each row, and returns the arithmetic mean of the non-blank results. Use AVERAGEX when the value you want to average requires per-row calculation — for example, averaging a profit margin that must be computed as Profit / Revenue for each row before averaging. AVERAGE(column) only works on a stored column of values; AVERAGEX computes on the fly.

examples.label: Average order value per transaction
examples.expression: Avg Order Value = AVERAGEX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * Sales[UnitPrice])
examples.explanation: Row O1: 2 × 500 = 1000. Row O2: 3 × 80 = 240. Row O3: 1 × 30 = 30. Average = (1000 + 240 + 30) / 3 = 423.33. Note: SUM(Sales[Qty]) * SUM(Sales[UnitPrice]) / COUNTROWS(Sales) would give a wrong result because it multiplies totals before dividing.

examples.label: AVERAGEX vs AVERAGE comparison
examples.explanation: AVERAGE(Sales[Amount]) returns (100 + 200) / 2 = 150 because blank rows are excluded. AVERAGEX(Sales, Sales[Amount]) also returns 150 for the same reason. The difference appears only when the expression produces blanks differently than the column's stored blanks.

iteratorFlow.description: AVERAGEX visits each row of the Sales table, computes the expression in that row's context, excludes blanks, then divides the sum of results by the count of non-blank results.

commonTraps: AVERAGEX(Sales, Sales[Amount]) and AVERAGE(Sales[Amount]) produce the same result when the column has no blank rows. They differ when the row expression produces blanks differently than the stored column — blanks are excluded from both numerator and denominator.

AVERAGE([Profit] / [Revenue]) is NOT the same as AVERAGEX(Sales, Sales[Profit] / Sales[Revenue]). The former takes the average of already-aggregated values; the latter computes a per-row ratio first, which is the correct approach for margin averaging.
If ALL rows produce BLANK, AVERAGEX returns BLANK — not zero or an error.

sqlEquivalent.note: SQL AVG() of an inline expression (AVG(Qty * UnitPrice)) computes per-row before averaging — exactly what AVERAGEX does. SQL also excludes NULLs from AVG automatically, mirroring AVERAGEX's blank-exclusion behavior.
